item.research_question: How does grain size influence the tribological behavior, wear mechanisms, and wear resistance of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloys under varying normal loads and sliding speeds?
item.material_system: CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) with fine grain (FG, ~2.9 μm) and coarse grain (CG, ~63.4 μm) microstructures
item.processing_route: Arc-melting of pure metals followed by drop-casting into a copper mold, forging at 1000 °C, cold rolling (80% reduction), and annealing at 800 °C for 30 min (FG) or 1000 °C for 60 min (CG)
item.test_conditions: Reciprocating sliding friction against a 10 mm Si3N4 ball under dry conditions at room temperature; normal loads of 5 N and 30 N; sliding speeds of 1, 5, and 10 mm/s; sliding time of 1200 s
key_findings: The average grain size was 2.9 μm for the fine grain (FG) sample and 63.4 μm for the coarse grain (CG) sample.
The hardness of the FG sample was approximately 4.9 GPa, significantly higher than the CG sample's 3.4 GPa.
Under low load (5 N) and low speed (1 mm/s), the primary wear mechanism for both samples was adhesive wear.
With increased sliding speed, the wear mechanisms evolved to include adhesive wear and oxidation wear.
Under high load (30 N) and high speed, the wear mechanisms included adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation.
The specific wear rate of the FG sample was significantly lower than that of the CG sample across all tested conditions.
The oxide layer formed on the CG sample surface was prone to cracking and fracture, whereas the FG sample's oxide layer remained more intact.
Increasing the normal load from 5 N to 30 N resulted in a decrease in the friction coefficient due to the formation of a lubricating oxide layer.
item.mechanism: The fine grain size provides higher surface strength and hardness, which improves wear resistance. Under friction heat, coarse grain samples soften more easily, causing their oxide layers to fracture and leading to increased wear. At high loads, the formation of a continuous oxide layer acts as a lubricant, reducing the friction coefficient, but the durability of this layer depends on the grain size and resulting hardness.
quotes: The fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.
The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG.
The hardness of FG and CG sample is approximately 4.9 GPa and 3.4 GPa, respectively.
